source.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
source.authors: Adam Karvonen; C. Rager; Johnny Lin; Curt Tigges; J. Bloom; David Chanin; Yeu-Tong Lau; Eoin Farrell; Callum McDougall; K. Ayonrinde; Demian Till; M. Wearden; Arthur Conmy; Samuel Marks; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature absorption across SAE widths, sparsity levels, and architectures. These results refine the splitting/absorption claims, but it does not directly track whether larger-dictionary latents partition the inputs or directions of particular smaller-dictionary latents.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses feature splitting and cites prior work, but does not directly match features across dictionary sizes or measure their input coverage and directional similarity. Rows below concern the study's own feature-absorption metric and its reported scaling trends, not direct evidence of feature splitting.
record.test_reason: The study applies a modified version of Chanin et al.'s first-letter absorption metric to over 200 SAEs. It varies dictionary width (4k–65k, plus Gemma-Scope 16k–1M), L0 and architecture, so its results bear on V4's claim that size and sparsity changes don't fix absorption. It never measures feature splitting itself: no cross-size latent matching, input partition, or direction similarity. Its link from splitting to inverse scaling is stated only as a hypothesis.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. Larger dictionaries improve reconstruction and auto-interp scores but worsen concept isolation (absorption, SCR, TPP) in non-hierarchical SAEs. Gemma-Scope shows the same trends up to 1M width. Matryoshka is the only architecture that improves with scale on disentanglement and shows minor absorption degradation. The authors hypothesize, without testing, that feature splitting drives this inverse scaling. Higher L0 reduces absorption, and moderate L0 of 50–150 is a reasonable compromise.
record.recipe_differences: The study benchmarks absorption and other SAE metrics across trained architectures and widths; it does not replicate the original feature-matching or input-partition analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-absorption results vary with dictionary width, L0 sparsity, and SAE architecture; the Gemma-Scope evaluation also spans model layers.

fits_no_version.finding: The hierarchical Matryoshka objective gives the best absorption scores among seven architectures. The authors report hierarchical SAEs beat others by 30–40% on absorption and SCR. All other architectures beat ReLU on absorption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Absorption depends on the SAE training objective: nested or hierarchical objectives substantially reduce it compared with standard sparse objectives.

record.problems: The absorption results are metric-level proxies, not direct tests of feature splitting or parent-child activation partitioning. Several scaling conclusions are stated qualitatively or summarized across architectures/layers without separate numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows needed; the reported relevant trends are recorded as aggregate results where the paper describes them in aggregate.

untested.parts: All of it. No matching of coarse features to finer ones across dictionary sizes, no input-coverage test, no direction similarity.
All of it. Gemma-Scope widths up to 1M are evaluated, but only on benchmark metrics, not on splitting correspondence.
All of it. No feature-family or geometry analysis.
There is no inspection of individual parent latents failing where child latents fire; absorption is inferred from probe projections. Only the first-letter hierarchy is used.
All of it. No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.
All of it. Splitting is never measured, so no evidence is given on whether Matryoshka or other objectives change splitting. The splitting explanation is offered only as a hypothesis.

missing.what: Absorption levels compared across architectures at a fixed 65k width: Matryoshka best, ReLU worst, p-anneal above Gated. This shows how much the architecture or objective affects absorption.
Absorption results on Pythia-160M, which the authors say show 'substantially different patterns' from Gemma-2-2B. This is a model-dependence condition for the absorption scaling results.

record.verdict_notes: The absorption metric (1 − absorption score) adapts Chanin et al. by using probe projections instead of ablation effects and by allowing partial and multi-latent absorption. Its feature-split detection uses τfs=0.03 k-sparse probing, which is a selection step, not a splitting measurement. The V6 links on R1/R2 were removed because splitting itself is never measured. Values are mostly qualitative text readings of figures.

versions.untested_parts: No direct smaller-to-larger feature matching, input-set partition test, or directional-similarity measurement.
The study evaluates scaling and open SAE releases, but does not test whether the specified coarse-to-fine feature correspondence holds in those settings.
No nested feature-family or geometrical-closeness analysis.

Measures absorption scores and their variation with width, sparsity, and architecture, but does not track a specific parent latent failing to fire when a child fires or isolate hierarchical parent-child pairs.
No decomposition of larger latents into smaller-latent combinations or count of novel larger-SAE latents.

Compares measured absorption across SAE architectures, including Matryoshka, but does not establish that splitting is caused by the training objective rather than reflecting model representations, or directly measure feature splitting.

relation.reason: Its width, L0 and architecture sweeps of absorption bear directly on V4.

tranche.reason: Uses a modified version of Chanin et al.'s first-letter absorption metric (probe projection, partial absorption, no ablation) across widths, L0 and architectures, so it is a different method on the same question. T5 is arguable for the L0 result, but the main width result supports V4.

source_check.notes: Same group as the original (shares 4 authors). Only first-letter absorption is measured, with no splitting measure. The authors' tie to feature splitting is a hypothesis they do not test. Appendix I states the Gemma-Scope trends with no numbers, and Figs 15 and 16 are both captioned Gemma-2-9B layer 20. The authors say Pythia-160M absorption patterns differ substantially from Gemma-2-2B. Matryoshka is 'often not superior' at L0 > 200.

statements.correction: arXiv:2503.09532 (Appendix, Feature Absorption): manual inspection found absorption often partial; the absorbed latent 'isn't completely suppressed, but still activates weakly', and several absorbing latents often share the compensation. No numbers are given. Its metric scores absorption as a fraction to capture this. The reported results are still an aggregate first-letter score.
statements.problem: Puts arXiv:2503.09532 only under 'aggregate probe score, not observed parent firing'. But the text reports from manual inspection that absorption is often partial, with the parent still firing weakly, which is the issue's own point.

statements.correction: Rows for this study: R4 (Gemma-2-2B Gemma Scope 16k-1M), R5 (Gemma-2-9B 16k-1M), R1 (own suite 4k-65k, non-Matryoshka), R2 (Matryoshka minor degradation).
statements.problem: Minor citation gap only: the Gemma-2-2B 16k-to-1M worsening is row R4, which is not cited. R1, which is cited, is the own-suite 4k-to-65k sweep.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Non-Matryoshka SAEs in the Gemma-2-2B width sweep and the Gemma-Scope width-series evaluations
reader_labels.reason: Absorption scores worsen with larger dictionaries in the reported non-Matryoshka sweep and degrade at larger widths in the Gemma-Scope series (R1, R4, R5). This is evidence of persistent or increased absorption, not direct evidence about specific parent-child latents.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Matryoshka scaling and changes in L0
reader_labels.reason: Matryoshka has only minor absorption-score degradation with width, and higher L0 reduces measured absorption; the study does not show whether either change fully removes absorption (R2, R3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Measured absorption in the Gemma-2-2B SAE architecture comparison
reader_labels.reason: Matryoshka is an exception to the usual worsening of absorption scores with scale, showing only minor degradation; this supports a difference in the measured absorption outcome across architectures, without establishing an objective-caused splitting artifact (R1, R2).
